items.followUp: State two properties of ionic compounds.

rubric.why: Coordinate covalent compounds generally share the physical properties of covalent compounds.
rubric.description: Identifies their generally low melting and boiling points.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating both low melting point and low boiling point.

rubric.why: Covalent compounds generally lack mobile charged particles.
rubric.description: States that they generally do not conduct electricity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that they do not, or poorly, conduct electricity.

modelAnswer: Coordinate covalent compounds generally have low melting and boiling points.
They generally do not conduct electricity because they lack mobile charged particles.

items.followUp: Define the boiling point of a substance.

rubric.why: Freezing is the change of state that defines the freezing point.
rubric.description: Identifies the change from liquid to solid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a liquid changes into a solid.

rubric.why: The freezing point is specified as a temperature, conventionally at atmospheric pressure.
rubric.description: Identifies the freezing point as the temperature of this change.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is the temperature at which the liquid solidifies; accept a reference to atmospheric pressure.

modelAnswer: The freezing point is the temperature at which a liquid changes into a solid.
It is usually specified at atmospheric pressure.

items.followUp: Define effusion and distinguish it from diffusion.

rubric.why: Diffusion is the spontaneous mixing or spreading of particles.
rubric.description: Describes diffusion as the movement or mixing of particles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the spontaneous movement or mixing of particles.

rubric.why: Diffusion proceeds down a concentration gradient.
rubric.description: States the direction of particle movement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that particles move from higher to lower concentration.

modelAnswer: Diffusion is the spontaneous movement and mixing of particles.
Particles move from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.

items.followUp: How does increasing temperature affect the rate of diffusion?

rubric.why: Intermolecular attractions hinder particle movement and spreading.
rubric.description: Links stronger intermolecular forces with slower diffusion, or weaker forces with faster diffusion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct relationship between force strength and diffusion rate.

rubric.why: The effect on diffusion occurs because intermolecular forces affect how freely particles can move.
rubric.description: Explains that intermolecular forces resist or restrict particle movement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining the effect of intermolecular forces on particle movement.

modelAnswer: Strong intermolecular forces hold particles together and slow their diffusion.
Weak intermolecular forces allow particles to move more freely, so diffusion is faster.

items.followUp: What is the boiling point of a liquid?

rubric.why: Melting is the change of state that defines the melting point.
rubric.description: Identifies the change from solid to liquid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a solid changes into a liquid.

rubric.why: The melting point is specified as the temperature of this change, conventionally at atmospheric pressure.
rubric.description: Defines the melting point as the temperature at which the solid melts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is the temperature at which a solid changes into a liquid; accept a reference to atmospheric pressure.

modelAnswer: The melting point is the temperature at which a solid changes into a liquid.
It is usually specified at atmospheric pressure.

items.followUp: Why do gases expand to fill their containers?

rubric.why: Gas particles are widely separated compared with particles in liquids and solids.
rubric.description: States that gas particles are far apart.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the large spaces between gas particles.

rubric.why: Widely spaced particles give a gas a small mass per unit volume.
rubric.description: Connects the particle spacing to the lower density of gases.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that this results in low density or low mass per unit volume.

modelAnswer: Gas particles are much farther apart than particles in liquids and solids.
Therefore, a given volume of gas contains less matter and has a lower density.

items.followUp: Write two differences between a suspension and a colloid.

rubric.why: A true solution is homogeneous, whereas a colloid is microscopically heterogeneous.
rubric.description: Distinguishes a solution from a colloid by uniformity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a solution as homogeneous and a colloid as heterogeneous.

rubric.why: Solution particles are smaller than colloidal particles; the usual textbook size ranges are below 1 nm for solutions and about 1–1000 nm for colloids.
rubric.description: Gives a particle-size difference between solutions and colloids.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct comparison of particle sizes, including the standard size ranges.

modelAnswer: A solution is homogeneous, whereas a colloid is heterogeneous on the microscopic level.
Solution particles are smaller than 1 nm, whereas colloidal particles are about 1–1000 nm in size.

items.followUp: Use the idea of polarity to explain why water dissolves sugar but not oil.

rubric.why: The rule describes the matching of solute and solvent properties, especially polarity.
rubric.description: Explains that substances with similar nature or polarity tend to dissolve in one another.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating the like-dissolves-like rule.

rubric.why: An example demonstrates the rule by pairing substances of similar polarity.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable example of matching solute and solvent types.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable example, such as polar water dissolving salt or nonpolar oil dissolving a nonpolar substance.

modelAnswer: “Like dissolves like” means that substances with similar polarity tend to dissolve in one another.
For example, polar water dissolves ionic salt, while nonpolar solvents dissolve nonpolar substances.
